rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate gradient duration and temperature provide a useful baseline for subsequent slope and selectivity tests.

Shorten only the gradient to measure how the critical pairs respond to slope while targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. This isolates slope effects before changing temperature to address pairs that remain unresolved.

The near-coeluting late pair barely responded to gradient slope, so test a substantial temperature change to shift selectivity. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature effects and should preserve the favorable run time.

Test lower temperature to improve the early critical pair, while a slightly shallower gradient should help the middle and late clusters. The previous runs suggest the last peak will remain close to the 10-minute scoring threshold.

Raise the starting organic fraction and narrow the gradient window to spend less time before the main peak cluster while using a shallower slope. This should improve slope-sensitive pairs while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes; the early peaks will be checked for compression.

Further narrow and shift the gradient window to improve the remaining slope-sensitive pairs without extending the last peak much beyond 10 minutes. The early pairs currently have enough resolution to test the compression caused by a higher starting organic fraction.

Lower the starting fraction one step to recover separation in the middle pair and protect the early cluster. This intermediate gradient should retain much of the late-cluster improvement while placing the last peak close to 10 minutes.

Test temperature at the best gradient window to see whether the nearly coincident late pair separates more effectively under shallower-gradient conditions. This also measures the trade-off between late-cluster selectivity and the remaining middle-pair resolution.

Test a substantially narrower window at the more favorable low temperature to improve the late cluster and probe whether its near-coelution can be shifted. This also establishes how much early- and middle-peak resolution is sacrificed by raising the starting organic fraction.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 6 to improve the middle and late critical pairs, with the last peak targeted near 10 minutes. Ending at 0.65 also tests whether a short terminal hold changes selectivity in the late cluster.

Retain the promising starting fraction from injection 10 but extend the gradient beyond the last peak to avoid terminal-hold broadening and delay. The slightly shallower slope should improve the remaining critical pairs, with the last peak expected near the 10-minute threshold.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 11, using a 5 °C temperature increase to keep the last peak below 10 minutes. This probes whether added gradient resolution outweighs the modest selectivity loss from warming.

Test a different regime in which the late cluster elutes during the final hold rather than the gradient, potentially changing its persistent near-coelution. The stronger initial ramp limits time spent reaching the hold, while the low temperature preserves early-pair selectivity.

Use one exploratory run to test a much steeper gradient, which may move critical pairs through selectivity crossings into a different separation pattern. The low starting fraction protects early retention, and the broad endpoint avoids a prolonged terminal hold.

Test a shallower gradient with enough temperature compensation to keep the last peak near 10 minutes. This explores whether stronger slope-driven separation can offset the selectivity losses seen when temperature alone was raised.

Explore a higher-starting, shallower-gradient regime to see whether the compressed early pair crosses and separates again while the late cluster gains resolution. This is a selectivity probe outside the local optimum; injection 7 remains the benchmark.

Refine the best method with a single 5 °C temperature step, checking for a local selectivity improvement that the larger temperature change may have missed. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates this effect and provides additional margin below 10 minutes.

Refine the lower-starting window with a slope between injections 5 and 7, aiming to bring the middle critical pairs above 1.5. The endpoint should keep the final peak inside the gradient, with retention close to the 10-minute scoring boundary.

Test the next shallower slope near injection 11 at the favorable low temperature. This will establish whether improved critical-pair resolution can compensate for the small expected time penalty just beyond 10 minutes.

Refine the 0.35 starting-fraction branch with a slightly shallower slope than injection 9, targeting the last peak near 10 minutes. This tests whether gains in the middle and late critical pairs can overcome the early-pair deficit.

Check the remaining lower-starting window near the 10-minute boundary, where improved middle-pair selectivity might offset weaker late-cluster resolution. This brackets the optimum from the lower-organic side while retaining the favorable temperature.

Apply the smallest temperature increase to injection 11 to remove its slight time penalty while retaining its favorable slope. This directly tests the closest remaining local competitor to the best method.

Test the high-temperature endpoint in the best gradient window for selectivity crossings beyond the unfavorable intermediate temperatures. The run should remain below 10 minutes; injection 7 remains the benchmark if those crossings do not improve resolution.

Test a slope between injections 6 and 11, keeping the endpoint high enough for the last peak to elute during the gradient. This targets improved critical-pair resolution over injection 6 without the time penalty of injection 11.

Use the final injection to test a shallower slope at the best starting fraction, with temperature compensation targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. This checks whether slope-driven gains can outweigh the selectivity losses observed when warming the best gradient alone.
